presidents.name: Millard Fillmore
presidents.summary: Fillmore became president in July 1850 and signed the Fugitive Slave Act on September 18, 1850, as part of the Compromise of 1850. He then used federal power to enforce it, including a February 18, 1851 proclamation ordering prosecution of the men who rescued Shadrach Minkins from federal custody in Boston.
presidents.paragraph: Fillmore took office when Zachary Taylor died, and within two months he'd signed the Fugitive Slave Act, approved September 18, 1850. The statute told federal commissioners to decide who was a fugitive, and it shut the accused out of the proceeding: "In no trial or hearing under this act shall the testimony of such alleged fugitive be admitted in evidence." Anyone who helped a person escape faced a fine up to a thousand dollars and up to six months in jail. The Miller Center records that Fillmore "believed the South would secede" without such a law, and that he used patronage to appoint officials who'd enforce it. He didn't leave enforcement to chance. After a crowd freed Shadrach Minkins from the Boston Court-House on February 15, 1851, Fillmore issued a proclamation three days later describing "sundry lawless persons, principally persons of color," and directing "that prosecutions be commenced against all persons who shall have made themselves aiders or abettors."

callouts.text: September 18, 1850: signed the Fugitive Slave Act (9 Stat. 462), which barred an accused fugitive's own testimony and penalized anyone aiding escape with fines up to $1,000 and six months' imprisonment.

presidents.personalRecord: No documentary record found in the sources fetched showing that Fillmore ever enslaved anyone. The Miller Center records that he came from a "desperately poor" family and was himself bound as an apprentice to a cloth maker — an arrangement the Miller Center says "amounted to little more than slavery" — and that he borrowed thirty dollars to buy out the indenture. The same source says he "was also opposed to slavery in principle but thought that compromise was essential." Nothing about his estate at death was verified from the sources fetched; treat any figure as UNVERIFIED.

presidents.name: Franklin Pierce
presidents.summary: Pierce signed the Kansas-Nebraska Act on May 30, 1854, which declared the Missouri Compromise restriction on slavery "inoperative and void" and left the question to territorial settlers. He also backed federal enforcement of the Fugitive Slave Act in the Anthony Burns case in Boston that same month, telegraphing the U.S. marshal that the law must be executed.
presidents.paragraph: Pierce's signature on the Kansas-Nebraska Act, May 30, 1854, undid the line drawn in 1820. The act declared the 1820 restriction "inoperative and void" and said its intent was "to leave the people thereof perfectly free to form and regulate their domestic institutions in their own way." The Miller Center records that the Kansas territory then "devolves into a guerilla war between pro-slavery and anti-slavery settlers," with roughly 200 dead over two years. The same spring, federal marshals in Boston arrested Anthony Burns, who'd escaped from Virginia. Pierce wired Marshal Watson Freeman on May 27, 1854: "Your conduct is approved. The law must be executed." Four days later he told the U.S. attorney to "incur any expense deemed necessary." The Massachusetts Historical Society records that on June 2 an estimated 50,000 people filled Court Square and State Street while marshals, soldiers, marines and militia marched Burns to the harbor. Before his presidency, the Miller Center says, Pierce "upheld the right of Americans to own property, even human property."

presidents.personalRecord: No documentary record found in the sources fetched showing that Pierce ever enslaved anyone; he was a New Hampshire native. The Miller Center records that before the presidency "only one cause seemed to inspire any real passion in him: opposition to the abolitionist movement," that he "remained firmly opposed to the abolition of slavery in the states where it already existed," and that he "upheld the right of Americans to own property, even human property." Nothing about his estate at death was verified from the sources fetched; treat any figure as UNVERIFIED.

presidents.name: James Buchanan
presidents.summary: In his March 4, 1857 inaugural address Buchanan said the territorial slavery question was pending before the Supreme Court and would be "speedily and finally settled," and pledged to "cheerfully submit" to the ruling. Two days later the Court decided Dred Scott v. Sandford; documented correspondence shows Buchanan had privately written to Justice Robert Grier beforehand.
presidents.paragraph: Two days before the Dred Scott ruling, Buchanan stood at his inauguration and called the territorial slavery question "a judicial question, which legitimately belongs to the Supreme Court of the United States, before whom it is now pending, and will, it is understood, be speedily and finally settled." He added that he would "cheerfully submit." He already knew more than he let on. In a letter dated February 23, 1857, Justice Robert Cooper Grier told Buchanan he had "taken the liberty to shew it in confidence to our mutual friends Judge Wayne and the Chief Justice," and that "six if not seven" justices would hold the 1820 compromise law of no effect. On March 6, 1857, Taney's opinion held that the act of Congress barring slavery north of the line "is not warranted by the Constitution, and is therefore void," and described Black people as having been regarded as "beings of an inferior order" with "no rights which the white man was bound to respect." Buchanan then backed the pro-slavery Lecompton constitution for Kansas.

presidents.personalRecord: Buchanan is the one lifelong bachelor president. The White House Historical Association records that in March 1835 a deed of transfer brought Daphne Cook, age twenty-two, and her daughter Ann Cook, age five, into Buchanan's possession in Pennsylvania: "Daphne, age twenty-two, would serve Buchanan for seven years while her daughter Ann Cook, age five, would serve for twenty-three years until she reached the age of twenty-eight." The WHHA notes historians question whether they were really indentured servants "or rather term slaves," and records that Ann died about three months later and Daphne ran away about two weeks after her daughter's death, with no record of what followed. Buchanan's nephew James Buchanan Henry claimed in 1911 that his uncle bought people's freedom in Washington, D.C.; the WHHA states that "to this date, direct evidence of Buchanan purchasing and freeing enslaved people while living in Washington, D.C. has not been found." His estate at death was not verified from sources fetched.

disputes: Buchanan's holding of the Cooks: Philip Klein's 1962 biography frames the March 1835 transaction as purchase-and-manumission and a "win-win"; the White House Historical Association notes the twenty-three-year term for a five-year-old and the absence of other options for the Cooks "calls into question whether Daphne and Ann were really indentured servants or rather term slaves." Both readings recorded.

Klein's timing: Klein casts the sale as defusing pre-election "political dynamite," but the WHHA points out the sale occurred in March 1835, three months after Buchanan's December 6, 1834 Senate election.

Whether Buchanan bought and freed enslaved people in Washington, D.C.: asserted by his nephew James Buchanan Henry in 1911; the WHHA says no direct evidence has been found and some historians think Henry relocated the Cook episode.

presidents.name: Abraham Lincoln
presidents.summary: Lincoln signed the District of Columbia Compensated Emancipation Act on April 16, 1862, issued the Emancipation Proclamation effective January 1, 1863, and approved the joint resolution sending the Thirteenth Amendment to the states on February 1, 1865. His stated position shifted over the war, from prioritizing the Union in August 1862 to publicly favoring limited Black suffrage on April 11, 1865.
presidents.paragraph: Lincoln's record moves. On April 16, 1862, he signed the act ending slavery in the District of Columbia; the National Archives records that commissioners went on to approve 930 petitions freeing 2,989 people, with former owners paid up to $300 each and up to $100 available to any freed person choosing to emigrate. On January 1, 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation declared that "all persons held as slaves within said designated States, and parts of States, are, and henceforward shall be free," and said such persons "will be received into the armed service of the United States." It applied to areas in rebellion and excepted parts of Louisiana and Virginia. Congress passed the Thirteenth Amendment on January 31, 1865, and Lincoln approved the resolution the next day; it was ratified December 6, 1865. In his last public address, April 11, 1865, speaking about the vote for Black men in Louisiana, he said: "I would myself prefer that it were now conferred on the very intelligent, and on those who serve our cause as soldiers."

presidents.name: Andrew Johnson
presidents.summary: Johnson vetoed the Freedmen's Bureau extension bill on February 19, 1866 and the Civil Rights Act on March 27, 1866, the latter overridden by Congress on April 9, 1866. His pardon policy and Bureau Circular No. 15 of September 12, 1865 set up the restoration of abandoned lands to pardoned former Confederate owners, and the House impeached him on February 24, 1868.
presidents.paragraph: Johnson's May 29, 1865 amnesty proclamation offered pardon to white southerners who took a loyalty oath, excluding high Confederate officials and planters with property over $20,000. On September 12, 1865, Bureau Circular No. 15 — drawn up at the White House — rescinded Howard's earlier Circular No. 13 and laid out how pardoned owners could apply to get abandoned lands back. Then came the vetoes. On February 19, 1866, he rejected the Freedmen's Bureau extension, objecting that it would "take away land from its former owners without any legal proceedings" and asserting freed people "can attain to that condition only through their own merits and exertions." On March 27, 1866, he vetoed the Civil Rights Act, writing that "the distinction of race and color is by the bill made to operate in favor of the colored and against the white race." Congress overrode him on April 9. In his December 3, 1867 annual message he wrote that "Negroes have shown less capacity for government than any other race of people." The House impeached him February 24, 1868; the Senate acquitted by one vote.

presidents.personalRecord: Johnson enslaved people. The National Park Service records that on November 29 he "paid $541.00 for Sam, a youth 'about thirteen years of age'"; on January 3, 1843 he "paid $500.00 to purchase Sam's half-sister, Dolly," then "about nineteen"; and on May 6, 1857 he "paid $1015.00 for Henry, another youth 'about thirteen years of age.'" NPS also names children born into that household — Dolly's children Liz, Florence and William, and Sam's children Dora, Robert and Hattie. On the freeing, NPS is explicit that the date rests on family tradition, not a document: "According to family lore, Andrew Johnson freed all his personal slaves on August 8, 1863." August 8 is still observed as Emancipation Day in East Tennessee. His estate at death was not verified from the sources fetched.

disputes: The August 8, 1863 emancipation of Johnson's own enslaved household: NPS attributes the date to "family lore" rather than a document, while regional Emancipation Day observance treats it as established. Both recorded.

Senate acquittal vote count and dates: the Senate's own page records 35–19 on Article 11 on May 16, 1868 and again on Articles 2 and 3 on May 26, 1868; the Miller Center page fetched gives only May 16, 1868, 35–19. No conflict in the numbers, but the May 26 votes are omitted from the Miller Center summary.

Number of people Johnson enslaved: NPS's purchase records document Sam, Dolly and Henry plus children born into the household; search summaries cite census counts of five in 1850 and 1860. The census figures were not confirmed on the NPS page.
unverified: 1850 and 1860 census counts of people enslaved by Johnson (search-summary only; not on the fetched NPS page).
Exact year of the November 29 purchase of Sam — the fetched NPS text gives the month and day but the year was not captured.
Johnson's 1867 Reconstruction Act vetoes and their override dates (not fetched).
